title: Chapter 3 Quiz 1
description: The kinds of data a program can handle, and the difference between a constant and a variable.
instructions: Take your time: read each question carefully, then check your answer.

questions.question: Which data type can only hold the value **True** or **False**?
questions.explanation: A Boolean holds one of two values: True or False.

questions.question: Which data type holds whole numbers such as 97 or -20?
questions.explanation: Integers are whole numeric values, signed or unsigned.

questions.question: Which data type fits the value 2.15?
questions.explanation: Real numbers have a fractional part. They are stored with a mantissa and an exponent.

questions.question: What is a **String**?
options: A value that is True or False
A set of numbers of the same type
questions.explanation: A string is a set of characters, for example 'COURSE'. A single character is one byte matching an ASCII code.

questions.question: Match each value to its data type.
questions.explanation: Each value has a natural type: True is Boolean, -15 whole, 3.14 real, 'b' one character, 'COURSE' a string.

questions.question: What is a **constant**?
options: A name given to a function
A set of data of the same type
Data that can change while the program runs
Data used by a program that cannot be modified
questions.explanation: A constant keeps its value for the whole program. Pi is a classic example.

questions.question: What is a **variable**?
options: Data used by a program that can be modified
questions.explanation: A variable can receive new values while the program runs.

questions.question: A variable can hold which of these?
options: The final result of a calculation
questions.explanation: The course lists three roles: input data, intermediate results and final results.

questions.question: A data array is a set of data of the same type.
questions.explanation: An array groups values of one type, such as an array of integers.

questions.question: All data is encoded in {{1}} in the computer's memory.
questions.explanation: Everything in memory is encoded in bytes.
